criterion_notes.c1: Touches on water supply and sanitary sewage collection coverage in the São Paulo Macrometropolis (SPMM) as descriptive regional background (Table 1, using SNIS 2018 data) and notes residential sewage network connections as one component of SABESP's role in the Córrego Limpo urban stream depollution program, although its second case (Cantareira System) concerns raw-water bulk abstraction grants rather than household sanitation access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, this paper would pass Criterion 2 ('yes') because it examines institutional, regulatory, and multi-level governance arrangements in the sanitation and water sectors (federative division of competences, municipal sanitation plans/councils/funds, and horizontal/vertical integration and citizen participation). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism clarification, it fails Criterion 2 ('no'): it examines macro-governance architecture, municipal planning adoption, collaborative urban river depollution (Córrego Limpo), and watershed committee negotiations over bulk raw-water abstraction permits (which the authors explicitly state on p. 13 regulate raw water resources rather than access to basic sanitation), rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, connection discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory rules analyzed in relation to service access). Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, however, the paper is still excluded due to lack of an analyzed service-access outcome and empirical access design (c4 and c5).
criterion_notes.c3: Borderline/unclear: the authors compute descriptive regional aggregations from secondary administrative databases across the 174 SPMM municipalities (SNIS 2018 coverage indicators in Table 1 and Figure 1; IBGE MUNIC 2017 self-reported counts of municipal sanitation plans, councils, and funds in Figure 2), but the core analysis of the two governance cases (Córrego Limpo and Cantareira System) relies on official documents and narrative synthesis of secondary academic theses/articles (p. 16; Chart 1) with no primary data collection, no systematic synthesis method, and no empirical analysis of service access.
criterion_notes.c4: No analyzed service-access outcome: aggregate SPMM water supply and sewage collection coverage figures from SNIS 2018 (Table 1) are presented solely as static descriptive background to characterize the policy problem (Chart 1, p. 4) and are never linked to or analyzed against any governance variable. The study's actual evaluated outcomes (Figure 2 and Chart 2) are municipal planning/council counts and governance process dimensions (horizontal integration, vertical integration, citizen participation, and territoriality).
criterion_notes.c5: Does not provide an identifiable empirical study design linking a governance exposure to a household or community water/sanitation service-access outcome; unit of analysis shifts across macro-regional descriptive totals, municipal planning counts, and secondary institutional case summaries of stream depollution and bulk water permitting.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English (pp. 1-21), with Portuguese and Spanish abstracts (pp. 22-23); English is directly eligible without translation.

study_design: Qualitative institutional and documentary policy analysis combining descriptive secondary administrative tabulations (SNIS 2018; IBGE MUNIC 2017) with narrative synthesis of secondary academic case studies
population_and_sample: São Paulo Macrometropolis (SPMM), encompassing 174 municipalities (~34.0 million inhabitants in SNIS/IBGE 2018), and two institutional governance cases (Córrego Limpo Program in São Paulo city and the Cantareira System water-granting renewal)
exposure: Multi-level environmental sanitation governance arrangements (federative competence distribution, municipal sanitation plans/councils/funds, horizontal and vertical integration, citizen participation, and territoriality in the Córrego Limpo urban stream depollution program and Cantareira System raw-water abstraction permitting)
outcome: Institutional governance process dimensions (horizontal integration, vertical integration, citizen participation, and territoriality) and municipal sanitation plan/council adoption; SNIS 2018 regional water and sewage coverage figures appear only as unanalyzed background context
rationale: Excluded primarily under E03 (Wrong exposure): under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, the paper examines macro-level multi-level governance architecture, federative competence sharing, municipal sanitation plan adoption, collaborative urban stream depollution (Córrego Limpo), and watershed committee negotiations over bulk raw-water abstraction permits (Cantareira System), rather than a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access. Furthermore, even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = 'exclude'), the paper remains ineligible because aggregate SNIS 2018 water and sewage coverage figures (Table 1) are presented only as static problem-framing background and are never analyzed in relation to any governance factor, while the study's evaluated outcomes (Chart 2, Figure 2) are governance process characteristics (horizontal/vertical integration, citizen participation, territoriality, and municipal planning) synthesized from official documents and secondary academic literature (c4 = no, c5 = no).
